title: A Bow, a Song, a Circle
bigQuestion: How did capoeira go from a crime in Brazil's law books to a treasure honored by Brazil and the world?

story.title: The Instrument on the Wall
story.kicker: In a school in Salvador, a berimbau hangs where a law once said the game was a crime.
paragraphs: Salvador is a port city in the state of Bahia, in northeast Brazil. In its old center, called the Pelourinho, there are capoeira schools up narrow stairs. On one wall hangs a berimbau, a wooden bow with one wire string and a gourd.

Beside the berimbau hang old black-and-white photographs. They show teachers who played capoeira in the early 1900s. Some of them played it when the law of Brazil called capoeira a crime. The police could arrest a person for it.

Today the same city has signs for tourists that point to capoeira schools. In 2014, UNESCO, a world body for education and culture, honored the capoeira circle. It added the circle to its list of treasures that people keep alive by doing them.
How does an art go from a police record to a world list? This chapter follows capoeira through old paintings, Brazilian laws, two famous teachers in Salvador and the schools they opened.
story.think: What might the old photographs on the wall teach a new student about the school's history?

lessons.title: Africans in Colonial Brazil
lessons.mainIdea: Capoeira grew among enslaved Africans and their children in Brazil, which was a colony of Portugal.
reading: Portugal ruled Brazil as a *colony* from the 1500s until 1822. Portuguese owners forced millions of Africans across the Atlantic Ocean. They made them work on sugar farms, in gold mines and in city houses. Brazil took in more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas.

Many of these people came from Central Africa, from lands around today's Angola and Congo. Others came from West Africa. They brought their languages, songs, drums and games. In Brazil, they and their children made new traditions from them.

*Capoeira* is one of those traditions. It is an *Afro-Brazilian* art that joins music, a game between two players and fighting skill. Historians agree it grew in Brazil among Africans and their children. They still argue about which African games fed into it and where the name comes from.

words.d: a land ruled by another country far away
an Afro-Brazilian art that joins music, a game between two players and fighting skill
made by Africans and their children in Brazil, or by Brazilians with African roots

look.title: Two Questions Historians Ask
look.text: Question one: Did capoeira grow in Brazil among Africans and their children? Most historians say yes, and many records back them. Question two: Which African game was its grandparent? Historians give different answers, and the records are thin.
look.prompt: Why might historians agree on the first question but not the second?

check.q: Which country ruled Brazil as a colony until 1822?
check.why: Portugal ruled Brazil as a colony from the 1500s until 1822.

check.q: What does Afro-Brazilian mean?
choices: made by Africans and their children in Brazil
made in Africa and never changed
check.why: Afro-Brazilian means made by Africans and their children in Brazil, or by Brazilians with African roots.

check.q: What do historians still argue about?
choices: which African games fed into capoeira
check.why: Historians agree capoeira grew in Brazil, but they still argue about its exact African roots and its name.

lessons.title: A Painter's Record
lessons.mainIdea: A picture made by the painter Johann Moritz Rugendas, printed in 1835, is one of the oldest images of capoeira.
reading: Johann Moritz Rugendas was a painter from Germany. He traveled in Brazil in the 1820s. He drew cities, forests, farms and the people he met. Later, his pictures were printed in a book about his trip, published in 1835.

One picture has the title Jogar Capoëra, which means "to play capoeira" in Portuguese. It shows two Black men facing each other in the middle of a group. People stand around them and watch. One man plays a drum. Rugendas also gave the picture a French title that called it a war dance.

The picture is a *primary source*, a record made at the time. It shows that people played capoeira in a circle with music by the 1820s. But it was made by an outsider. Historians read it carefully, because a visitor may not have known what he was seeing.

words.d: a record made at the time, such as a picture, a letter or a law
Johann Moritz Rugendas, a German painter who pictured capoeira in Brazil in the 1820s

look.title: Reading the Picture

check.why: Johann Moritz Rugendas was a German painter who traveled in Brazil.

check.q: What is a primary source?

check.why: A primary source is made at the time, like Rugendas's picture from his trip.

lessons.title: Capoeira in Police Records
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, police in Rio de Janeiro arrested people for capoeira, and their records are now sources for history.
reading: Rio de Janeiro was Brazil's capital for most of the 1800s. It was a busy port full of enslaved and free Black workers. City leaders feared groups of capoeira players on the streets. Police arrested people for playing capoeira, even before a national law named it.

Police wrote down each arrest in record books. The books list names, dates and the reason for the arrest. Historians have searched these books to learn who played capoeira. Many of those arrested were enslaved men. Others were free Black workers, and some were poor immigrants.

The records also name street groups called *maltas*. Two large groups in Rio were the Nagoas and the Guaiamuns. They controlled different parts of the city. Police records tell us about them, but they tell the story from the side of the police.

words.d: a street group of capoeira players in Rio de Janeiro in the 1800s
when police take a person away because they say the person broke a rule or law

look.title: One Line in a Record Book
look.text: Imagine one line in an old police book from Rio de Janeiro. It gives a man's first name, the day and the words "for capoeira." It does not say what he felt, who taught him or what songs he knew.
look.prompt: What does this line tell a historian, and whose voice is missing from it?

check.q: What were maltas?
choices: street groups of capoeira players in Rio
check.why: Police records in Rio name maltas, street groups of capoeira players, such as the Nagoas and Guaiamuns.

check.q: Who wrote the police records?
check.why: Police wrote the arrest books, so the records show the story from the police side.

check.q: Which city was Brazil's capital for most of the 1800s?
check.why: Rio de Janeiro was the capital for most of the 1800s.

lessons.title: The Golden Law of 1888
lessons.mainIdea: Brazil ended slavery on May 13, 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so.
reading: For more than 300 years, slavery was legal in Brazil. Enslaved people fought it in many ways. Some ran away and built free towns called quilombos. The most famous, Palmares, lasted for most of the 1600s.

On May 13, 1888, Princess Isabel signed the *Golden Law*. In Portuguese it is called the Lei Áurea. It was very short. It said that slavery in Brazil was ended. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery.

The law did not give land, money or schooling to freed people. Many former enslaved people stayed poor. They moved to cities looking for work. Many capoeira players were among them, and city leaders soon aimed new laws at them.

words.d: the 1888 law, the Lei Áurea, that ended slavery in Brazil
a free town built in Brazil by people who escaped slavery

look.title: What the Law Left Out
look.text: A law of 1888 says slavery is ended. It says nothing about land, jobs, homes or schools. A freed woman now owns her own time. She still needs a place to live and a way to earn money.
look.prompt: What problems might freed people face when a law ends slavery but gives nothing else?

check.q: When did Brazil end slavery?
check.why: Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law on May 13, 1888.

check.q: What was a quilombo?
choices: a free town built by people who escaped slavery
check.why: Quilombos were free towns built by people who escaped slavery, such as Palmares.

check.q: What did the Golden Law NOT give freed people?
check.why: The law ended slavery but gave freed people no land, money or schooling.

lessons.title: The Penal Code of 1890
lessons.mainIdea: In 1890, Brazil's new Penal Code made playing capoeira in the streets a crime.
reading: In November 1889, Brazil stopped having an emperor. It became a *republic*, a country led by elected leaders. The new government wrote new laws quickly. In 1890 it published a *penal code*, the book of laws about crimes and punishments.

One chapter of the 1890 Penal Code was about people it called idle, and about capoeira players. Article 402 said that doing capoeira in streets and squares was a crime. The punishment was time in prison. Leaders of groups could be punished more.

The law was written only two years after slavery ended. It aimed at an art played mostly by Black Brazilians. Police used it to arrest players for decades. Many historians see it as one way the new republic tried to control Black city life.

words.d: a country led by elected leaders instead of a king or emperor
a country's book of laws about crimes and their punishments

look.title: Article 402
look.text: It is a crime to do, in streets and public squares, the exercises of skill and body movement known as capoeira. The punishment is prison.
look.cite: Brazil, Penal Code of 1890 (Código Penal dos Estados Unidos do Brasil), Article 402, retold in plain English
look.prompt: Where does this law say capoeira was a crime, and why do you think it named those places?

check.q: What is a penal code?
choices: a book of laws about crimes and punishments
check.why: A penal code lists crimes and their punishments; Brazil's 1890 code named capoeira.

check.q: What changed in Brazil in November 1889?
check.why: In November 1889 Brazil stopped having an emperor and became a republic.

check.q: According to Article 402, where was capoeira a crime?
check.why: Article 402 named capoeira done in streets and public squares.

lessons.title: Keeping the Game Alive
lessons.mainIdea: Players kept capoeira alive in yards and on docks until the law changed in 1940.
reading: The 1890 law did not stop capoeira. In Salvador, in the state of Bahia, players met in backyards, at docks and at street festivals. Many worked as dock workers, market sellers or builders. Older players taught younger ones by playing with them.

Many capoeira histories say players used *nicknames* in those years. A nickname made a player harder to find in police records. Today many capoeira groups still give students a nickname. Groups describe it as a link to that past.
In 1940, Brazil wrote a new penal code. The new code did not name capoeira as a crime. After 50 years, playing capoeira in the street was no longer against the national law.

words.d: a name used in place of a person's real name
a state in northeast Brazil; its capital, Salvador, is a center of capoeira

check.q: What happened to the capoeira crime in 1940?

check.why: Brazil's new penal code of 1940 no longer named capoeira as a crime.

lessons.title: Mestre Bimba's Academy
lessons.mainIdea: In Salvador in 1932, Mestre Bimba opened one of the first capoeira academies, with set lessons and rules.
reading: Manuel dos Reis Machado was born in Salvador in 1899. People called him *Mestre* Bimba. Mestre means master teacher in Portuguese. He said he learned capoeira as a boy from an African man who worked on ships.

In 1932, Bimba opened an *academy*, a school with a fixed room and set lessons. He called his style the Regional Fighting of Bahia. It later became known as Capoeira Regional. In 1937, the government of Bahia gave his school an official license.

Bimba's academy had rules for students. It kept a list of members and held graduations. Many of his first students were university students and middle-class men. They brought capoeira into rooms that had once kept it out. In 1953, Bimba and his students showed capoeira to President Getúlio Vargas.

words.d: the Portuguese word for master teacher, used for respected capoeira teachers
a school with a fixed room, set lessons and rules for students
the style of capoeira that Mestre Bimba built at his academy in Salvador

look.title: Two Places to Learn
look.text: Place one: a backyard in Salvador in 1910. No sign, no list of students, no fixed hours. An older player teaches by playing. Place two: Bimba's academy in 1937. A license from the state, a list of members, set lessons and a graduation day.
look.prompt: Name two things the academy had that the backyard did not. Why might a license matter after years of arrests?

check.q: What does the Portuguese word mestre mean?
check.why: Mestre means master teacher; Manuel dos Reis Machado was called Mestre Bimba.

check.q: When did Mestre Bimba open his academy?
check.why: Bimba opened his academy in Salvador in 1932, and it got an official license in 1937.

check.q: What style grew from Bimba's academy?
check.why: Bimba's Regional Fighting of Bahia became known as Capoeira Regional.

lessons.title: Mestre Pastinha and Angola
lessons.mainIdea: In 1941, Mestre Pastinha opened a center in Salvador to keep the older style, called Capoeira Angola.
reading: Vicente Ferreira Pastinha was born in Salvador in 1889. People called him Mestre Pastinha. He said he learned capoeira as a boy from an African man named Benedito. He also worked as a painter and a shoemaker.

In 1941, Pastinha opened the Sports Center of Capoeira Angola. It later moved to the Pelourinho, in Salvador's old center. *Capoeira Angola* is the name for the older style. The name honors Angola, in Central Africa, where many enslaved people had been taken from.

Pastinha wanted to keep the old songs, rituals and slow games. In 1964, he published a book called Capoeira Angola. In 1966, he led a group to Dakar, in Senegal, for the First World Festival of Negro Arts. He died in Salvador in 1981.

words.d: the name for the older style of capoeira, kept by Mestre Pastinha and his students
the old center of Salvador, Brazil, where Pastinha's school stood

look.title: Two Mestres, Two Goals
look.text: Mestre Bimba built a new style with set lessons and graduations. Mestre Pastinha set out to keep the older style, with its old songs and slow games. Both worked in Salvador. Both opened schools with a sign on the door.
look.prompt: How were Bimba's and Pastinha's goals different, and how were they alike?

check.why: Capoeira Angola honors Angola, in Central Africa, where many enslaved people had been taken from.

check.q: What did Pastinha want to keep?
choices: the old songs, rituals and slow games
check.why: Pastinha's school kept the older style of capoeira, with its old songs and rituals.

check.q: Where did Pastinha lead a group in 1966?
check.why: In 1966 Pastinha led a group to the First World Festival of Negro Arts in Dakar, Senegal.

lessons.title: Brazil Names a Treasure
lessons.mainIdea: Brazil named the capoeira circle a national treasure in 2008, and UNESCO added it to a world list in 2014.
reading: Brazil has a government office that protects its history and culture. It is called IPHAN. In 2008, IPHAN listed two parts of capoeira as Brazilian *cultural heritage*. One was the *roda*, the circle where capoeira is played. The other was the work of the mestres who teach it.

In 2014, UNESCO added the capoeira circle to its world list of intangible cultural heritage. Intangible means it is not an object you can hold. It lives in songs, games and teaching. UNESCO is part of the United Nations.

These honors came 118 years and 124 years after the 1890 law. The same circle that police once broke up is now protected. Capoeira groups say that mestres and players, not laws, kept it alive in between.

words.d: the customs, arts and places a people keeps and passes on
the circle of people where capoeira is played, with music
not an object you can touch; living in songs, skills and teaching

look.title: Two Documents, 124 Years Apart
look.text: Document one, 1890: a law says capoeira in streets and squares is a crime. Document two, 2014: a world body says the capoeira circle is a treasure that humanity should protect.
look.prompt: What changed between the two documents? Who do you think helped make that change?

check.q: What is the roda?
choices: the circle where capoeira is played
check.why: The roda is the circle of people, with music, where capoeira is played.

check.q: What did UNESCO do in 2014?
choices: it added the capoeira circle to a world heritage list
check.why: In 2014 UNESCO added the capoeira circle to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

check.q: What does intangible mean?
choices: not an object you can touch
check.why: Intangible heritage lives in songs, skills and teaching, not in objects.

lessons.title: Capoeira Travels the World
lessons.mainIdea: Starting in the 1970s, Brazilian mestres moved abroad and opened capoeira schools in many countries.
reading: In the 1970s, some Brazilian capoeira teachers moved to the United States and Europe. They taught in dance studios, colleges and community centers. By the 1990s, capoeira schools were open in many big cities around the world.

One teacher who moved was João Oliveira dos Santos, called Mestre João Grande. He had been a student of Mestre Pastinha in Salvador. He opened a Capoeira Angola school in New York City in the 1990s. In 2001, the National Endowment for the Arts gave him a National Heritage Fellowship.

Capoeira groups abroad often keep the Portuguese songs. Students learn Portuguese words to sing them. Many groups visit Salvador to meet the mestres. The circle that began in Brazil now meets in many languages, but the songs stay in Portuguese.

words.d: an honor from the U.S. National Endowment for the Arts for masters of folk and traditional arts
the main language of Brazil and of capoeira songs

look.text: A capoeira group meets in a city far from Brazil. Most students grew up speaking English. They sing in Portuguese. A photo of their teacher's teacher from Salvador hangs on the wall.
look.prompt: Why might a group so far from Brazil keep singing in Portuguese?
